What is the PCSB School Performance Report?
The DC Public Charter School Board (PCSB) produces a detailed annual performance report for each public
charter school it oversees. Each report includes information on the school’s performance on the Performance
Management Framework (PMF) for standard schools and an evaluation of the school’s accountability plan for non-
standard schools (early childhood, adult education, GED, and the school serving 100 percent special needs stu-
dents). Each report card provides a school profile, student demographics, and for standard schools, the school’s
rating in the three performance tiers. The report card also shows how students are progressing over time; how
they are achieving in reading and mathematics; how prepared students are for future success; and attendance
and re-enrollment rates in the school.
Included in this document are listings of the schools; the user guide, which explains how to read the report cards;
and each school’s performance report. For more information on how the metrics are calculated, please see the
PMF Guidelines and Technical Guide in the PMF section of the PCSB website, www.dcpubliccharter.com.
About the DC Public Charter School Board
The PCSB currently oversees 53 schools on 98 campuses, which serve more than 32,000 students from every
ward of the city. The organization’s mission is to provide high-quality public school options for District of Colum-
bia students, families, and communities through four functions:

schools in the nation’s capital. Our vision is that every DC student receives a quality
education that makes them feel valued and prepares them for lifelong learning, fulfilling
careers, and economic security. DC PCSB creates the policies and conditions that empower
educators to do their best work in serving students.

DC Public Charter School Board
Report on the Budgeted At-Risk Funding and Estimated Next
Year At-Risk Spending Plan in DC Public Charter Schools
under the Common Financial Reporting Standards (CFRS)
Fiscal Year (FY) 2023

Background and Introduction
As the sole public charter school authorizer in the nation’s capital, the DC Public
Charter School Board (DC PCSB) in FY 2023 is providing financial oversight to 135
public charter schools managed by 69 independently run nonprofit organizations
known as local education agencies (LEAs). Through this oversight, DC PCSB ensures
public dollars are being spent appropriately. However, this oversight is not subject to
individual expenditures and cannot mandate the types of at-risk funding utilization.
The oversight tracked by DC PCSB includes reviewing broad expenditures such as
contracts, personnel, facilities, and other uses of funds, including the DC Uniform Per
Student Funding Formula (UPSFF) funds. As part of its annual compliance reporting
to DC PCSB, each LEA must provide a summary of how it plans to spend its at-risk
funding.
Beginning in FY 2023, the requirements for completing and submitting the at-risk
reports have changed pursuant to D.C. Law 23-149 Fiscal Year 2021 Budget Support
Act of 2020 Sec. 4052. The at-risk reports that follow this section support the LEA’s
budget prepared in accordance with the Common Financial Reporting Standards
(CFRS).
The School Reform Act states that LEAs have exclusive control over their
“expenditures, administration, personnel, and instructional methods.” This allows
schools to use the at-risk funding they receive in a way that is most responsive to the
needs of at-risk students.

Around the start of each school year, the Office of the Deputy Mayor for Education
(DME) publishes the UPSFF weighting for each grade level and special population of
student, including at-risk students. The most recent DME’s UPSFF Payments
Memoranda informing this report can be found at 2021-22 UPSFF Payments and
Weightings and 2022-23 UPSFF Payments and Weightings. The Office of the State
Superintendent of Education (OSSE) provides the Office of the Chief Financial Officer
(OCFO) with audited enrollment data for each LEA to determine the amount of
at-risk funds to disburse to each LEA. The OCFO disburses the funds directly to each
LEA in accordance with the UPSFF Payments Memoranda.
The FY 2023 budgeted at-risk expenditure reports that follow this section also
include the FY 2023 budgeted at-risk student enrollment. The “Actual” column in
each at-risk expenditure report has been left blank, and the “Variance” column will
subtract the “Budget” at-risk expenditures from the “Actual” at-risk expenditures
when the “Actual” at-risk expenditures are entered after FY 2023 in connection with
OSSE’s CFRS actual expenditures collection from each LEA by March 2024.

DC Public Charter School Board
Discipline and Truancy Report
SY 2014-15
August 2015

Summary
In order for students to achieve academically, quality schools must create school
cultures and environments that promote appropriate student behaviors and
encourage consistent student attendance. As part of the DC Public Charter School
Board’s (PCSB) oversight over DC public charter schools, and pursuant to D.C.
Official Code § 38-203, PCSB tracks attendance data at all DC public charter schools
and annually publishes a report on that data. PCSB also annually reports on discipline
data and trends within public charter schools. The report makes publicly available
school-by-school data pertaining to the rates of student suspension and expulsion,
truancy and in-school attendance and analyzes trends in public charter school
attendance policies.
In school year 2014-15, the DC public charter school sector saw decreases in student
suspensions, expulsions and truancies as well as an increase in the in-seat attendance
rate from school year 2013-14. This continues a four-year positive trend for each of
these metrics. Specifically:
• Expulsions dropped from 139 (0.38% expulsion rate) in SY 2013-14 to 131
(0.35%) in SY 2014-15.
• Students with at least one out-of-school suspension also decreased, from
11.9% in SY 2013-14 to 10.9% in SY 2014-15
• In-seat attendance (for PK—12th) increased from 91.6% in SY 2013-14 to 92.0%
in SY 2014-15. Overall, these numbers mean an average of nearly 150
additional students per day attending public charter schools across the District.
PCSB does n

notified in real time when they reach attendance thresholds, rather than being
notified in quarterly reports, which encouraged schools to implement strategies more
expeditiously to address truancy concerns. The thresholds remained the same – 20%
for elementary/middle, 25% for high school and 35% for alternative schools.
During the upcoming school year (2015-16), PCSB plans to continue to improve
citywide and cross-agency coordination to address the issue of truancy. In particular,
PCSB has worked with OSSE and charter LEA’s to develop a new and streamlined
process for collecting and reporting truancy and discipline data. This will allow
charter LEA’s, PCSB and OSSE to more easily share data with each other and the
public, as well as more easily comply with the new reporting requirements in the Pre-
K Student Discipline Amendment Act of 2015.
The remainder of this report contains detailed information on PCSB’s discipline and
truancy data for SY 2014-15, including a presentation on PCSB’s truancy and
discipline data, campus-level data and an analysis of trends in public charter school
attendance policies.

Each year, the DC Public Charter School Board (DC PCSB) collaborates with the
Office of the State Superintendent (OSSE) and public charter local education

change after OSSE releases its annual attendance report in the fall. Comparative
data points from SY 2022-23 in this report reflect final school-certified data. DC PCSB

In SY 2023 – 24, the out-of-school suspension and expulsion rates stayed relatively
flat compared to the previous year, continuing to remain lower than in the years
before the pandemic. However, loss of instructional time due to suspensions
reduced by over half, indicating suspensions are getting shorter and students are
not losing unnecessary instructional time. This reduction compared to pre-
pandemic years is a testament to the sector’s commitment to minimizing the use of
punitive disciplinary measures in favor of more restorative practices. Schools have
increasingly adopted alternative approaches to discipline, aiming to address
underlying issues and promote positive behavioral changes.

DC PCSB will continue to engage with schools, monitor their progress, and
implement targeted oversight interventions as necessary. Additionally, as part of its
ongoing efforts to improve accountability and increase transparency, DC PCSB has
revised its academic accountability system to incorporate chronic absenteeism
(within grades K – 12) as a key school environment metric. Chronic absenteeism a
dynamic measure that depends on the changing proportion of absences relative to
instructional days. Chronic absenteeism includes excused, unexcused, partial, and

Moreover, DC PCSB’s academic accountability system disaggregates performance in
this measure by student group to spotlight the organization’s commitment to

Attendance and Discipline Report
School Year 2025 – 26

Summary
The District of Columbia Public Charter School Board (DC PCSB) is
responsible for providing oversight on the performance of DC public charter
schools, including monitoring whether students have consistent access to
instructional time. As part of that oversight, DC PCSB uses attendance and
discipline data collected by the Office of the State Superintendent of
Education (OSSE) and works with public charter local education agencies
(LEAs) to identify trends, understand emerging concerns, and support school
accountability. Attendance is an important measure of school performance
and student success. This annual report summarizes attendance and
discipline data for students enrolled in DC public charter schools during
school year (SY) 2025-26, pursuant to reporting requirements in D.C. Code §
38-203(i).
SY 2025-26 marks the 30th anniversary of the public charter school sector in
DC. In the past three decades, the sector has grown from a small number of
schools to more than 130 schools serving nearly half the District’s public
school students.
An already celebratory year, SY 2025-26 marks a notable improvement in the
sector’s attendance recovery since the COVID-19 pandemic. Across all major
attendance and discipline metrics included in this report—chronic
absenteeism, truancy, in-seat attendance, suspension rate, and expulsion
rate—results improved from the previous school year.
In January 2027, DC PCSB will publish ASPIRE scores and levels for public
charter schools for the

37.06%, compared with 39.92% in SY 2024–25. Rates continued to differ by
grade level, with high school students experiencing higher rates of chronic
absenteeism than students in elementary and middle grades.
Chronic truancy and in-seat attendance also remain critical attendance
measures. In SY 2025-26, the chronic truancy rate for the public charter sector
was 31.85%, compared with 33.19% in SY 2024-25, a decrease of 1.34 percentage
points. In SY 2025-26, the public charter sector’s in-seat attendance rate was
89.66%, compared with 89.20% in SY 2024-25.
Discipline outcomes similarly improved in SY 2025-26. The percentage of
students who received an out-of-school suspension decreased from 6.39% in
SY 2024-25 to 3.85% in SY 2025-26, while the expulsion rate decreased from
0.17% to 0.12%. The percentage of instructional time lost due to suspensions
also declined, from 0.18% to 0.11%.
Gains in attendance and discipline outcomes follow school staff increasing

Comparing SY 2025 – 26 to SY 2024 – 25 shows the following trends. Across all of the following metrics, the charter sector improved from the previous school year. ● Enrollment: by 0.58% (47,525 to 47,801) ● Suspensions: from 6.39% to 3.85% ● Expulsions: from 0.17% to 0.12% ● Lost Instruction Time: from 0.18% to 0.11% ● In Seat Attendance (PK – 12 only): from 89.20% to 89.66% ● Truancy (students ages 5 – 17 only): from 33.19% to 31.85% ● Chronic Absenteeism (PK – 12 only): from 39.32% to 37.06% DC PUBLIC CHARTER SCHOOL BOARD — PAGE 5
SY 2025 – 26 ATTENDANCE AND DISCIPLINE SCHOOL CAMPUS TRENDS DC PUBLIC CHARTER SCHOOL BOARD — PAGE 6
REFERRALS AND BARRIERS TO ATTENDANCE DC PUBLIC CHARTER SCHOOL BOARD — PAGE 14

Court Social Services and Child and Family Services Agency (CFSA) Referrals (Self-Reported Data) ● 3,764 students (ages 5 – 13) were referred for truancy to the DC Child and Family Services Agency (CFSA). ● 768 students (ages 14 – 17) were referred for truancy to DC’s Family Court Social Services Division (FCSSD). Student Support Team (Self-Reported Data) ● 14,430 DC public charter school students met with a Student Support Team (SST), or its equivalent, for attendance purposes in SY 2025 – 26. DC PUBLIC CHARTER SCHOOL BOARD — PAGE 15

● Automated & Milestone Notifications: Daily robocalls, text alerts via platforms like ParentSquare, and automated emails at specific absence thresholds (e.g., 4, 8, 10, or 12 days). ● Direct Outreach: Immediate calls and texts from teachers, attendance coordinators, or social workers following missed days, escalating to certified letters and home visits for chronic cases. ● Simplified Documentation: Online portals, pre-filled excuse forms, and daily attendance trackers to help families to submit valid absence documentation in required timelines. ● Attendance Action Plans & Contracts: Individualized contracts created with students and parents to establish clear attendance goals, morning routines, and progress tracking. ● Attendance Impact & Re-engagement Meetings: Formal conferences involving administrative leadership, social workers, deans, and counselors to identify causes and resolve personal barriers. ● Data-Driven Tracking: Weekly cross-departmental "Attendance Attack Team" or SST data dives using platforms like PowerSchool, Panorama, or PowerBI to monitor trends and assign case management responsibilities. DC PUBLIC CHARTER SCHOOL BOARD — PAGE 16

● Tangible Rewards & Events: Dress-down passes, field trips, school store tokens, "Glow Parties," ice cream socials, gift cards, and quarterly celebrations. ● Relational Initiatives: Programs like the "95% Attendance Club" or "Beat the 18," along with "Lunch Bunch" opportunities to build connections with trusted adults. ● Student & Family Recognition: Certificates, public acknowledgments, town hall spotlights, and parent-focused raffles. ● Transportation Solutions: Distribution of Kids Ride Free (KRF) SmarTrip cards, shuttle buses, Uber vouchers, private van pickups, and carpool coordination. ● Basic Needs & Stabilization: Providing free uniforms, outerwear, hygiene items, food distribution, and access to on-site laundry facilities. ● Flexible Supports: Alternative schedules for working students or teen parents, before/after-care placement, and access to devices/technology for learning continuity. DC PUBLIC CHARTER SCHOOL BOARD — PAGE 17

● Mentoring & Check-Ins: Assigning dedicated staff or adult mentors for daily "Check-In/Check-Out" routines and relationship building. ● Counseling & Social Work: In-house therapy, group SEL sessions (e.g., Second Step curriculum), and referrals to external behavioral health partners (e.g., Mary's Center, PASS, SHOW UP STAND OUT). ● Health Coordination: Connecting families with primary care providers, allergy management, or immunization clinics to prevent extended health-related absences. ● Remedial Opportunities: Mandatory tutoring sessions, high-dosage tutoring (HIT), after-school office hours, and homework clubs. ● Attendance Recovery Plans: Allowing students to catch up on missing work, receive assignment extensions, or complete modified coursework to maintain academic momentum.
